\chapter{Greetings}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Telugu, recognize the reply, and choose an appropriate response.}

The greetings and the words that oil a first conversation — and, taught through them, how to read the Telugu script and how Telugu sits inside the Dravidian family. Each word introduces the letters it needs, so you learn to read it and understand it at once: \te{నమస్కారం} · \te{ధన్యవాదములు} · \te{అవును} · \te{లేదు} · \te{సరే}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[namaskāram]{\te{నమస్కారం} (namaskāram) — \textquotedblleft{}greetings,\textquotedblright{} a making of a bow}

\label{lesson:TE-C01-namaskaram}



\begin{quote}
Meet your first Telugu word. Say \textbf{namaskāram} with a small bow: “hello” or “greetings.” Now read it one small piece at a time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Telugu runs \textbf{left to right}. A consonant normally carries a built-in \textbf{a}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{న} · \te{మ} · \te{ర}} = \emph{na · ma · ra}.
  \item \textbf{\te{కా}} = \textbf{\te{క}} \emph{ka} plus the long-\emph{ā} vowel sign: \emph{kā}.
  \item In \textbf{\te{స్క}}, \textbf{\te{స}} loses its vowel and stacks below \textbf{\te{క}}: \emph{s + ka = ska}.
  \item The dot \textbf{\te{ం}} adds the final nasal sound \emph{ṁ}.
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\te{న} · \te{మ} · \te{స్} · \te{కా} · \te{ర} · \te{ం}} = \emph{na-ma-s-kā-raṁ} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} = \textbf{namaskāram}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} came from Sanskrit \textbf{namas} (“a bow”) + \textbf{kāra} (“a making,” from \emph{kṛ}, “to do”): literally \textbf{“the making of a bow.”} Telugu added its own final sound. Tamil instead kept its native greeting, \emph{vaṇakkam}.

\textbf{Across the family — the same idea, six ways:}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Hello\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} & Sanskrit \\
Kannada & \emph{namaskāra} & Sanskrit — the same word \\
Malayalam & \emph{namaskāram} & Sanskrit — the same word \\
Hindi & \emph{namaste} & Sanskrit — the same \emph{namas} \\
Tamil & \emph{vaṇakkam} & \textbf{native Dravidian} \\
English & \emph{hello} & Germanic \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four of the six borrowed the Sanskrit bow. \textbf{Tamil alone kept its own word} — the first sign that \textquotedblleft{}Dravidian family\textquotedblright{} does not mean \textquotedblleft{}same vocabulary.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
With palms together and a small bow, \emph{namaskāram} works as \textbf{hello or goodbye}. It is respectful without being stiff.
\end{culture}

\begin{sounds}
Telugu reads \textbf{left to right}, and every consonant carries a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} (many under a little check-mark hat, the \emph{talakaṭṭu}). \te{న} \emph{na}, \te{మ} \emph{ma}, \te{ర} \emph{ra}. A \textbf{vowel sign} changes it: \te{క} \emph{ka} + long-ā $\to$ \te{కా} \emph{kā}. A vowel-less consonant \textbf{stacks below} the next as a conjunct: \te{స} tucks under \emph{ka} $\to$ \te{స్క} \textquotedblleft{}ska.\textquotedblright{} And the \textbf{anusvāra} \te{ం} adds a final nasal \textquotedblleft{}-ṁ.\textquotedblright{} Read \te{న}·\te{మ}·\te{స్}·\te{కా}·\te{ర}·\te{ం} $\to$ \emph{namaskāram}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} na · ma · s · kā · raṁ $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}namaskāram\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} what the anusvāra \te{ం} adds (a final nasal, \textquotedblleft{}-ṁ\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}namaskāram,\textquotedblright{} with a small bow
  \item \emph{Write it:} trace \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} with a finger, then copy it once
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}}. What does it mean? (“Greetings.”) What does the dot \textbf{\te{ం}} add? (A final nasal.) What does the whole word literally mean? (“The making of a bow.”)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhanyavādamulu]{\te{ధన్యవాదములు} (dhanyavādamulu) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} utterances of \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C01-dhanyavadamulu}



\begin{quote}
Another Sanskrit loan — and a first look at a Telugu \emph{ending}, the plural that turns \textquotedblleft{}a thanks\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}thanks.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ధ}} = \textquotedblleft{}dha\textquotedblright{} — an \textbf{aspirated} \emph{d} (a puff of breath after it).
  \item \textbf{\te{న్య}} = \textquotedblleft{}nya\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\te{న}} (na) vowel-stripped and stacked with \textbf{\te{య}} (ya).
  \item \textbf{\te{వా}} = \textquotedblleft{}vā\textquotedblright{} · \textbf{\te{ద}} = \textquotedblleft{}da\textquotedblright{} · \textbf{\te{ము}} = \textquotedblleft{}mu\textquotedblright{} · \textbf{\te{లు}} = \textquotedblleft{}lu.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\te{ధ} · \te{న్య} · \te{వా} · \te{ద} · \te{ము} · \te{లు}} = \emph{dha-nya-vā-da-mu-lu} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} = \textbf{dhanyavādamulu}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The core is \textbf{Sanskrit}: \textbf{dhanya} (\textquotedblleft{}worthy, blessed,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{dhana}, \textquotedblleft{}wealth\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{vāda} (\textquotedblleft{}a saying,\textquotedblright{} root \emph{vad}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}an utterance of '{[}you are{]} worthy.'\textquotedblright{} Telugu then adds its own \textbf{plural ending -mulu}, so \emph{dhanyavāda-mulu} is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}worthy-sayings,\textquotedblright{}} thanks in the plural of courtesy. (You'll also hear the shorter \emph{dhanyavādālu}.) The Sanskrit stem is the same one inside Hindi \emph{dhanyavād} and Kannada \emph{dhanyavāda}.

\textbf{Across the family — the same idea, five ways:}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Thanks\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Note} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Telugu} & \emph{dhanyavādamulu} (\te{ధన్యవాదములు}) & \textbf{Sanskrit} stem + Telugu plural \\
Kannada & \emph{dhanyavāda} (\ka{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}) & Sanskrit — same stem \\
Hindi & \emph{dhanyavād} (\dv{धन्यवाद}) & Sanskrit — same stem \\
Tamil & \emph{naṉṟi} (\ta{நன்றி}) & \textbf{native} (\textquotedblleft{}goodness\textquotedblright{}) \\
Malayalam & \emph{nandi} (\ml{നന്ദി}) & \textbf{native} — Tamil's cousin \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Telugu, Kannada, and Hindi share the Sanskrit stem; Tamil and Malayalam keep the native \emph{naṉṟi / nandi}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Telugu builds words by gluing endings on}]
\emph{-mulu} is your first taste of how Telugu (like all Dravidian languages) works: it is \textbf{agglutinative} — it stacks meaning by gluing endings onto a stem, one after another, rather than using separate little words. Here a plural rides on a borrowed Sanskrit noun. Later endings will mark case (\textquotedblleft{}to,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}from,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}with\textquotedblright{}) the same way. Bank the idea: in Telugu, grammar is mostly \textbf{suffixes}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
New: \te{ధ} \emph{dha} (aspirated \emph{d}), the conjunct \te{న్య} (\emph{na} stacked with \emph{ya}), then \te{వా}·\te{ద}·\te{ము}·\te{లు}. Read \te{ధ}·\te{న్య}·\te{వా}·\te{ద}·\te{ము}·\te{లు} $\to$ \emph{dhanyavādamulu}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item dha · nya · vā · da · mu · lu $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavādamulu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pieces — Sanskrit \emph{dhanya-vāda} + Telugu plural \emph{-mulu}
  \item the shorter everyday form, \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavādālu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}}. What is Sanskrit in it, and what is Telugu? (\emph{dhanya-vāda} is Sanskrit; the plural \emph{-mulu} is Telugu.) What does \textquotedblleft{}agglutinative\textquotedblright{} mean for how Telugu builds words? (It glues endings onto a stem.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ka]{\te{క} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S03-letter-ka}



\begin{quote}
Rounded, curvy letters, most crowned with a small tick or check-mark headstroke; no continuous top line. This is the first one.

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{క}}
\textbf{\te{క}} — \emph{ka}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{k}, it is \textbf{ka}.

You already say this one, and it has \te{క} inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{క} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{క} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{క} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{క} three times, saying \emph{ka} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{క} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{క}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ka}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[avunu]{\te{అవును} (avunu) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C01-avunu}



\begin{quote}
After two Sanskrit loans, a \textbf{native Telugu} word: the plain \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{అ}} = \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}} — an \textbf{independent vowel} (the word starts with a vowel, so it gets a full letter, not a hooked-on sign).
  \item \textbf{\te{వు}} = \textquotedblleft{}vu\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\te{వ}} (va) with the \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}u\textquotedblright{} vowel sign}.
  \item \textbf{\te{ను}} = \textquotedblleft{}nu\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\te{న}} (na) with the \textquotedblleft{}u\textquotedblright{} sign.
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\te{అ} · \te{వు} · \te{ను}} = \emph{a-vu-nu} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{అవును}} = \textbf{avunu} = \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{అవును}} (\emph{avunu}) is the everyday \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}yes / it is so,\textquotedblright{}} a native Telugu word. It comes from the verb of being — literally close to \textquotedblleft{}it is\textquotedblright{} — which is why the next lesson's \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kādu}, \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}) is its exact mirror.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: yes and no as \textquotedblleft{}it is\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}it is not\textquotedblright{}}]
Telugu's yes/no pair are really little \textbf{statements of being}: \emph{avunu} (\textquotedblleft{}it is {[}so{]}\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{kādu} (\textquotedblleft{}it is not\textquotedblright{}). This is a very Dravidian instinct — answer by asserting or denying existence, rather than with a bare particle. You'll also hear a \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} come back as the question's own verb, echoed (\emph{vaccānu}, \textquotedblleft{}I came,\textquotedblright{} for \textquotedblleft{}did you come?\textquotedblright{}). Bank \emph{avunu} as the simple word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\te{అ} is the \textbf{independent vowel} “a” (word-initial). \te{వు} is \emph{vu}, \te{ను} is \emph{nu} (each a consonant with the “u” sign). Read \te{అ}·\te{వు}·\te{ను} $\to$ \emph{avunu}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a · vu · nu $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}avunu\textquotedblright{}
  \item why \te{అ} is a full letter here (the word starts with the vowel)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}avunu\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}yes, it is so\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\te{అవును}}. Native Telugu or Sanskrit loan? (Native.) At root, what kind of statement is a Telugu \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}? (An assertion of being — \textquotedblleft{}it is {[}so{]},\textquotedblright{} mirrored by \emph{kādu}, \textquotedblleft{}it is not.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\te{◌ా} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S07-vowel-sign-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{క} — what does it do?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ా}}
\textbf{\te{◌ా}} — \emph{ā}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ā}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ా} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ా} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ా} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ా} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}  ·  \te{అవును}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ా} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ా} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ా}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ā} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lēdu]{\te{లేదు} (lēdu) — \textquotedblleft{}no,\textquotedblright{} where Telugu parts ways with its sisters}

\label{lesson:TE-C01-ledu}



\begin{quote}
The partner of \emph{avunu} — and a small surprise. Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam all say \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} with a word built on \emph{il-} (\emph{illai / illa}). Telugu does \textbf{not}: it goes its own way with \emph{lēdu}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{లే}} = \textquotedblleft{}lē\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\te{ల}} (la) with the \textbf{long-\textquotedblleft{}ē\textquotedblright{} vowel sign}.
  \item \textbf{\te{దు}} = \textquotedblleft{}du\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\te{ద}} (da) with the \textquotedblleft{}u\textquotedblright{} sign.
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\te{లే} · \te{దు}} = \emph{lē-du} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{లేదు}} = \textbf{lēdu}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{లేదు}} (\emph{lēdu}) means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}there is not, it is absent.\textquotedblright{}} It is native Dravidian, but built on a \textbf{different root} (\emph{lē-}, absence) from the \emph{il-} of Tamil and Kannada. Telugu also has \textbf{\te{కాదు}} (\emph{kādu}), \textquotedblleft{}it is \textbf{not} {[}that{]}\textquotedblright{} — so Telugu splits \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} into two:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{lēdu} — denies \textbf{existence} (\textquotedblleft{}there isn't\textquotedblright{}): \emph{pustakam lēdu}, \textquotedblleft{}there is no book.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{kādu} — denies \textbf{identity} (\textquotedblleft{}it isn't {[}that{]}\textquotedblright{}): \emph{idi pustakam kādu}, \textquotedblleft{}this is not a book.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Across the family — the same idea, five ways:}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}No / isn't\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Note} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Telugu} & \emph{lēdu} / \emph{kādu} (\te{లేదు} / \te{కాదు}) & native, but a \textbf{different root} (\emph{lē-}, \emph{kā-}) \\
Tamil & \emph{illai} (\ta{இல்லை}) & native, root \emph{il-} \\
Kannada & \emph{illa} (\ka{ಇಲ್ಲ}) & native, root \emph{il-} \\
Malayalam & \emph{illa} (\ml{ഇല്ല}) & native, root \emph{il-} \\
Hindi & \emph{nahīṁ} (\dv{नहीं}) & Indo-European (unrelated) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three sisters share \emph{il-}; Telugu alone picked \emph{lē-} / \emph{kā-}. Same family, not a uniform one — a reminder that Dravidian has real internal branches.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}s, existence vs. identity}]
English leans on one flat \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{} Telugu — carefully — keeps \textbf{two negatives}: \emph{lēdu} for \textquotedblleft{}there isn't / doesn't exist,\textquotedblright{} \emph{kādu} for \textquotedblleft{}is not {[}the thing you said{]}.\textquotedblright{} Choosing between them is choosing \emph{what} you're denying. (This two-way negative is a Dravidian trait; Tamil has an echo of it too, but Telugu draws the line most sharply — and with a different root-word from its sisters.)
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\te{లే} is \emph{lē} (\te{ల} \emph{la} with the long-“ē” sign); \te{దు} is \emph{du}. Read \te{లే}·\te{దు} $\to$ \emph{lēdu}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item lē · du $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}lēdu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \emph{avunu} (\textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) / \emph{lēdu} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{})
  \item the two no's — \emph{pustakam lēdu} (\textquotedblleft{}no book\textquotedblright{}) vs. \emph{idi pustakam kādu} (\textquotedblleft{}this isn't a book\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\te{లేదు}}. What does it deny — existence or identity? (Existence — \textquotedblleft{}there isn't\textquotedblright{}; \emph{kādu} denies identity.) How does Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} differ from Tamil's and Kannada's? (Different root: \emph{lē-} / \emph{kā-}, not the shared \emph{il-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sarē]{\te{సరే} (sarē) — \textquotedblleft{}okay,\textquotedblright{} the family word in Telugu dress}

\label{lesson:TE-C01-sare}



\begin{quote}
The easy middle between \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}: \textquotedblleft{}okay, alright, fine.\textquotedblright{} It's the same Dravidian word you'd meet as \emph{sari} in Tamil and Kannada — Telugu just rounds it off to \emph{sarē}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{స}} = \textquotedblleft{}sa.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\te{రే}} = \textquotedblleft{}rē\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\te{ర}} (ra) with the \textbf{long-\textquotedblleft{}ē\textquotedblright{} vowel sign} (the same sign you met on \emph{lē} in \emph{lēdu}).
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\te{స} · \te{రే}} = \emph{sa-rē} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{సరే}} = \textbf{sarē} = \textquotedblleft{}okay / alright.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{సరే}} (\emph{sarē}) is native Dravidian \textquotedblleft{}correct, right $\to$ okay, agreed\textquotedblright{} — the verbal nod of Telugu. It is the same family word as Tamil and Kannada \textbf{\te{సరి}/\ka{ಸರಿ}/\ta{சரி}} (\emph{sari}), worn to \emph{sarē} in Telugu. Say it once to agree; say \emph{sarē sarē} to mean \textquotedblleft{}yes yes, fine, enough.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one Dravidian word, three scripts}]
\emph{sari / sarē} is a clean demonstration of family closeness: essentially one word, one meaning, dressed in three different scripts — Tamil, Kannada, Telugu. As you learn to read each, spotting a shared word shift its shape but not its sense is the quickest way to feel the relationship (and the whole reason to learn these four side by side).
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\te{స} is \emph{sa}; \te{రే} is \emph{rē} (\te{ర} \emph{ra} with the long-“ē” sign you just met on \emph{lē}). Read \te{స}·\te{రే} $\to$ \emph{sarē}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sa · rē $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}sarē\textquotedblright{}
  \item the everyday triple — \emph{avunu} (yes) · \emph{lēdu} (no) · \emph{sarē} (okay)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sarē sarē\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}alright, alright\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\te{సరే}}. What does it mean, and what is its Tamil/Kannada twin? (\textquotedblleft{}Okay, agreed\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sari}.) Which vowel sign does \emph{rē} share with \emph{lēdu}? (The long-\textquotedblleft{}ē\textquotedblright{} sign.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ē]{\te{◌ే} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S120-vowel-sign-ee}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ా} — what does it do?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ే}}
\textbf{\te{◌ే}} — \emph{ē}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ē}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ే} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{లేదు}} \emph{lēdu} — no / there isn't (lēdu)
  \item \textbf{\te{సరే}} \emph{sarē} — okay / alright (sarē)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ే} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ే} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ే} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{లేదు}  ·  \te{సరే}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ే} three times, saying \emph{ē} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ే} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ే}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ē} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — a five-word recap}

\label{lesson:TE-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
Five words, and a first handful of Telugu letters read straight off the page. Let's gather only what you have already learned and make it feel easy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — read them back}
Sound each out, left to right, before checking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Read} & \textbf{} & \textbf{Meaning} & \textbf{Origin} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} & \emph{namaskāram} & hello / greetings & Sanskrit \\
\textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} & \emph{dhanyavādamulu} & thank you & Sanskrit stem + Telugu plural \\
\textbf{\te{అవును}} & \emph{avunu} & yes & native \\
\textbf{\te{లేదు}} & \emph{lēdu} & no / there isn't & native (root \emph{lē-}, not \emph{il-}) \\
\textbf{\te{సరే}} & \emph{sarē} & okay & native (= \emph{sari}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The letters that did it: consonants carry a built-in \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}} (many under the little \emph{talakaṭṭu} hat); a \textbf{vowel sign} swaps that vowel (\te{ా} ā, \te{ు} u, \te{ే} ē); a \textbf{virama} lets a consonant \textbf{stack below} the next as a conjunct (\te{స్క}); a dot \textbf{anusvāra} (\te{ం}) adds a final nasal; and a word-initial vowel gets a \textbf{full letter} (\te{అ}).

The now-familiar pattern: the two \textbf{greeting/politeness} words are Sanskrit; the three \textbf{everyday grammar} words are native — though Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} (\emph{lēdu}) takes a \emph{different} native root from its sisters' \emph{il-}.

\begin{culture}
Telugu has a warm departure exchange built around going and coming back. It belongs in the later chapter where you learn those actions one at a time. For now, repeating the greeting is enough when you part.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five — namaskāram · dhanyavādamulu · avunu · lēdu · sarē
  \item greet and thank — \textquotedblleft{}namaskāram!\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavādamulu.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read all five aloud. Which two are Sanskrit, which three native? (Sanskrit: \emph{namaskāram}, \emph{dhanyavādamulu}. Native: \emph{avunu}, \emph{lēdu}, \emph{sarē}.) How does Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} differ from its sisters'? (Different root — \emph{lē-} / \emph{kā-}, not \emph{il-}.) Which word means \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{sarē}.)

Next chapter starts introducing yourself, one short possession form at a time.
\end{tcolorbox}
